analysis.one_liner: Bars large companies from charging consumers more than a tariff actually costs them.
analysis.headline: Introduced November 28, 2025 with 24 Democratic cosponsors, sent to three House committees, and untouched since — no hearing, markup, or floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill makes it unlawful for any seller to raise the price of a tariffed good above the actual cost the tariff added, plus other documented business costs — but not costs like bigger executive pay or stock buybacks. Companies whose parent earns under $100 million a year from U.S. goods sales are exempt, so the rule aims at big retailers and importers. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce it, state attorneys general could sue on shoppers' behalf, consumers could report suspected gouging, and two agencies would publish yearly reports tracking prices of tariffed goods. It covers goods hit by tariffs that took effect on or after January 20, 2025, and even goods tariffs are only announced for, so sellers cannot raise prices in anticipation of a tariff. [S2]
analysis.who_benefits: Shoppers buying goods touched by the 2025 tariffs — appliances, electronics, groceries, and anything assembled in the U.S. with imported parts — would be protected from price increases that go beyond what the tariff itself costs a company. Large companies would bear the burden of proving their price increases match real tariff and business costs. [S2]

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits selling a tariffed good at a price raised by more than the costs directly generated by the tariff, plus other documented costs, with executive compensation and share buyback costs explicitly excluded as justifications. [S2]
Covers not only final goods hit by tariffs but also goods assembled in the U.S. with tariffed components, and goods a tariff has merely been announced for, blocking preemptive price hikes. [S2]

Lets state attorneys general sue for damages, restitution, or injunctions on behalf of residents, and requires the FTC to set up a consumer reporting hotline, website, and mailing address within 180 days of enactment. [S2]

Requires annual public reports from the International Trade Commission and Bureau of Labor Statistics tracking price changes at companies with $1 billion or more in revenue, focused on tariffed goods. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Large retailers and importers — the bill exempts companies whose ultimate parent earns under $100 million a year from U.S. goods sales — would face FTC enforcement, penalties, state lawsuits, and a rebuttable presumption of violation during tariff shock periods if they hold market power and raise prices above their pre-tariff baseline. They would have to document and justify price increases. [S2]

drawbacks.text: The bill does not lower the tariff cost itself: companies may still pass the full tariff onto shoppers, so consumers still pay more — the bill only stops increases beyond that. [S2]

The compliance burden is heavy: sellers must calculate a 180-day pre-tariff baseline price and demonstrate by clear and convincing evidence that increases match tariff and other documented costs, which could make companies hesitant to adjust prices for unrelated cost changes. [S2]
The $100 million revenue exemption creates a sharp cutoff — a company just above the line faces full enforcement while one just below is untouched. [S2]

Economists have long argued that price-gouging rules can discourage sellers from stocking goods when costs spike, since they cannot freely reprice; a five-year restriction across all tariffed goods is a longer and broader price control than typical emergency gouging bans.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core promise is real: during a period of sweeping tariffs, it stops billion-dollar companies from using tariffs as cover for larger price increases, and it preserves state enforcement and consumer reporting. The costs are regulatory complexity, a five-year window that outlasts any tariff emergency, and the fact that it leaves the tariff burden itself untouched — shoppers still absorb every dollar of actual tariff cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced and nothing has happened since — no hearing, markup, or vote — while Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro and seven other Democrats introduced the bill on November 28, 2025. [S2]
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Workforce committees. [S4]
Twenty-four Democrats signed on as cosponsors; no further action has been taken on the bill. [S3]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large retailers and importers are better off so far: with no committee action, they keep full freedom to price above tariff costs. Consumers still face whatever prices companies choose.

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill prohibiting price gouging on tariffed goods.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Workforce Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on November 28, 2025 and have taken no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 24 cosponsors are House Democrats; no Republican cosponsors appear in the record, and the Republican-led committees have not acted on the bill.

industries.industry: Large retailers and consumer goods importers
industries.note: The bill strips companies with over $100 million in U.S. goods revenue of the ability to raise prices beyond documented tariff costs, with a presumption of violation for $1 billion firms during tariff shock periods. Their gain from tariff-covered price increases is directly shoppers' cost.

industries.industry: Small businesses (under $100 million U.S. goods revenue)
industries.note: They are explicitly exempt, facing none of the enforcement or recordkeeping burden, and could gain customers if large firms' prices are constrained.

industries.industry: Household goods and appliance makers using imported components
industries.note: The bill covers U.S.-assembled goods with tariffed components, limiting their pricing room, but they may still pass through actual tariff costs and could compete on price against larger rivals.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors, three committee referrals, and no movement since late November, the bill faces the usual fate of a minority-party pricing bill: it is very unlikely to get a hearing or a floor vote in this Congress unless leadership changes course.
